name: Tikal National Park
blurb: Maya-forest fruit trees, spider monkeys and jaguars above the ancient city.

tip.title: Thin the ramon trees
tip.text: Ramon fruit and seeds feed monkeys, agoutis, deer, turkeys and toucans. Set Ramon (breadnut) to -100% and watch those animals, then the jaguar and puma that hunt them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sapodilla
nodes.desc: A common forest tree of the Maya lowlands whose sweet fruit is eaten by fruit bats and other animals.

nodes.name: Kapok tree
nodes.desc: A giant emergent tree, sacred to the Maya. Fruit bats feed on its flowers and fruit.
A common tree whose small fruits are eaten by many birds, bats and monkeys.
Fruit makes up most of its feeding time, with young leaves as the main extra. Jaguars and pumas are its main likely predators.
A ground rodent that eats fruit and seeds and stores seeds when food is plentiful, making it an important seed disperser.
Feeds on fruit of sapodilla, kapok, gumbo-limbo and other trees, carrying seeds as it flies.
A ground-feeding omnivore of the Yucatan region eating insects such as leafcutter ants, plus seeds, nuts and leaves. It roosts high in trees, partly to avoid jaguars.
A large-billed fruit eater of the canopy that spreads seeds of the trees it feeds on.
Common in the park. They cut leaves to feed a fungus garden and are themselves eaten by ocellated turkeys and coatis.
An omnivore that forages on the ground and in trees for insects, small vertebrates, eggs, fruit and carrion.
A scavenger that cleans up carcasses; GloBI records show it feeding on deer and agouti.

nodes.name: Terciopelo (fer-de-lance)
nodes.desc: A large venomous pit viper; GloBI records show it eating agoutis and climbing rats.
A spotted cat that mostly hunts small mammals under about a kilogram, along with birds and reptiles. Jaguars and pumas can kill adults.
The largest cat of the Americas and a top predator of the forest, taking deer, peccaries and other prey, including ocellated turkeys.
A large cat that roams the park alongside the jaguar; spider monkeys are likely prey.
Year-round tropical light drives the growth of the forest canopy.
The seasonal rains feed the forest and refill the low swampy ground.

nodes.name: Fungi & litter decomposers
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, fruit and carcasses and return nutrients to the forest soil.
